scenes.title: A wonderful arrival
scenes.poem: I had gone a-begging from door to door in the village path when thy golden chariot appeared in the distance like a gorgeous dream and I wondered who was this king of all kings!

scenes.title: Great expectations
scenes.poem: My hopes rose high and me thought my evil days were at an end, and I stood waiting for alms to be given unasked and for wealth scattered on all sides in the dust.

scenes.title: The king stops
scenes.poem: The chariot stopped where I stood. Thy glance fell on me and thou camest down with a smile. I felt that the luck of my life had come at last.

scenes.title: An unexpected question
scenes.poem: Then of a sudden thou didst hold out thy right hand and say “What hast thou to give to me?”

scenes.title: Confusion and hesitation
scenes.poem: Ah, what a kingly jest was it to open thy palm to a beggar to beg! I was confused and stood undecided,

scenes.title: The smallest gift
scenes.poem: and then from my wallet I slowly took out the least little grain of corn and gave it to thee.

scenes.title: A discovery at day’s end
scenes.poem: But how great my surprise when at the day’s end I emptied my bag on the floor to find a least little grain of gold among the poor heap.

scenes.title: Regret
scenes.poem: I bitterly wept and wished that I had the heart to give thee my all.

beats.text: Imagine you are hoping someone will help you.
But when that person arrives, they ask you for something instead.
How would you feel?
Today, we are reading ‘A Little Grain of Gold’ by Rabindranath Tagore.
We will read it a little at a time, picture what happens, and explore what the story means.
The speaker is the person telling the story.
Here, he is a man who survives by asking others for help.
When he says ‘I’, we hear this character's voice.
You will notice some old-fashioned words.
‘Thou’ and ‘thee’ mean ‘you’.
‘Thy’ means ‘your’.
Keep those meanings in mind as we begin.
I had gone a-begging from door to door
in the village path
when thy golden chariot appeared in the distance
like a gorgeous dream
and I wondered who was this king of all kings!
The speaker has been going from house to house, asking for help.
‘A-begging’ simply means begging.
Suddenly, he sees a magnificent golden chariot.
A chariot is a vehicle pulled by horses.
‘Gorgeous’ means very beautiful.
The chariot seems so wonderful that he compares it to a beautiful dream.
Notice the word ‘like’: it helps us spot a simile, a comparison between two different things.
The speaker wonders who this ‘king of all kings’ could be.
That phrase makes the visitor seem greater than an ordinary king.
We will return to its deeper meaning later.
My hopes rose high
and me thought my evil days were at an end,
and I stood waiting for alms to be given unasked
and for wealth scattered on all sides in the dust.
Seeing the king, the speaker hopes his difficult life is about to change.
‘Me thought’ means ‘it seemed to me’.
His ‘evil days’ are his days of suffering and hardship.
The phrase does not mean that he is an evil person.
‘Alms’ are gifts, such as food or money, given to people in need.
‘Unasked’ means without his even having to ask.
He imagines so much wealth that it will be scattered everywhere.
This is what he hopes for; it has not happened.
At this point, he is thinking about what he will receive.
The chariot stopped where I stood.
Thy glance fell on me
and thou camest down with a smile.
I felt that the luck of my life had come at last.
The chariot stops exactly where the speaker is standing.
The king looks at him, comes down, and smiles.
‘Thy glance fell on me’ means ‘you looked at me’.
Nothing literally falls!
‘Thou camest down’ means ‘you came down’.
The king's friendly attention makes the speaker even more hopeful.
He feels that his great moment of good fortune has finally arrived.
So far, everything seems to support his expectation of receiving a gift.
Then of a sudden thou didst hold out thy right hand
and say
“What hast thou to give to me?”
Suddenly, the king holds out his hand.
‘Thou didst’ means ‘you did’, and ‘hast’ means ‘have’.
His question means, ‘What do you have to give me?’
Stop and think: why is this so surprising?
The speaker expected the rich king to give something to him.
Instead, the king asks him to give.
Their expected roles have been reversed.
This surprising contrast is an example of irony.
Ah, what a kingly jest was it
to open thy palm to a beggar to beg!
I was confused and stood undecided,
A ‘jest’ is a joke.
‘Kingly’ means royal, or belonging to a king.
The speaker thinks this must be a strange royal joke: a king asking a beggar for something!
That is the speaker's reaction.
The poem does not say that the king is laughing at him.
‘Undecided’ means he cannot make up his mind.
He pauses, unsure what to do.
His hope has changed into confusion.
The sentence continues with the choice he finally makes.
and then from my wallet
I slowly took out the least little grain of corn
and gave it to thee.
Here, ‘wallet’ means a small bag or pouch.
‘Corn’ refers to grain.
He takes out the smallest little grain and gives it to the king.
Which words tell us that he is reluctant to give?
‘Slowly’ suggests hesitation.
‘Least little’ stresses how tiny his gift is.
He does give something, but he holds back almost everything.
We can understand that someone with very little may worry about losing it.
The poem asks us to notice this particular choice: he hopes to receive generously, but finds it difficult to give generously.
But how great my surprise
when at the day’s end I emptied my bag on the floor
to find a least little grain of gold
among the poor heap.
At the end of the day, the speaker empties his bag and discovers a tiny grain of gold among his few possessions.
That small collection is the ‘poor heap’.
Remember ‘the least little grain of corn’?
Now we hear ‘a least little grain of gold’.
The repeated words connect his tiny gift with the precious thing he finds.
The poem suggests that what he gave has returned to him in a more precious form.
We are told about his discovery; we are not shown the moment of any transformation.
I bitterly wept
and wished that I had the heart
to give thee my all.
‘Bitterly wept’ means cried with deep sorrow.
‘Had the heart’ means had the willingness or generosity.
‘My all’ means everything I had.
Why does he feel sad after finding something valuable?
He realises that he held back.
On the story's surface, he may wish he had given more because even his tiny gift brought something precious.
More deeply, he regrets missing the chance to give wholeheartedly.
Notice what he wishes for: the heart to give.
His regret concerns his attitude as well as the size of his gift.
The ending leaves us thinking about the opportunity he has missed.
The textbook invites us to read this poem as a parable.
A parable is a simple story that teaches a moral or spiritual lesson.
In this spiritual reading, the ‘king of all kings’ represents God.
The speaker can represent a human being who asks for blessings but struggles to give.
The king's request can be understood as an invitation to generosity and trust.
A symbol is something in a story that also suggests a bigger idea.
The small grain can represent what we are willing to offer.
The gold can represent the precious value of giving, including spiritual richness.
Does this mean that giving a pencil will make a gold pencil appear?
No.
This is a story with a deeper meaning, not a promise of material rewards.
Its lesson is to give sincerely, without treating kindness as a bargain.
For us, generosity can include sharing our time, helping someone understand a lesson, or offering something we can spare.
The poem asks us to think about the willingness behind the gift.
Let's notice three choices that make the poem effective.
First, the simile ‘like a gorgeous dream’ compares the golden chariot to a wonderful dream, using ‘like’.
It helps us imagine the speaker's wonder.
Second, the king asks the beggar for a gift.
This reversal of what we expect creates irony and makes us stop and think.
Third, the words ‘least little grain’ connect the small gift with the small piece of gold.
Their repetition helps us understand the speaker's regret.
The title brings us back to that tiny piece of gold.
It is small in size, but it leads to a big discovery about giving.
Let's check our understanding.
Say your answer aloud, or pause the video if you need more time.
One: where did the chariot stop, and who came down?
It stopped where the speaker was standing, and the king came down with a smile.
Two: explain ‘kingly jest’.
Why did the speaker think the request was a joke?
It means a royal joke.
He was confused because he expected the wealthy king to give him something, but the king asked him for a gift instead.
Three: why was the speaker both surprised and sorrowful at the end?
He was surprised to find a tiny grain of gold.
He was sorrowful because he had given so little and wished he had been generous enough to give his all.
When you write an answer, explain the idea and support it with a phrase from the poem.
For the final question, ‘the least little grain’ and ‘had the heart to give’ are useful evidence.
Follow the speaker's feelings one last time.
He hopes to receive.
He is confused by the king's request.
He gives reluctantly, discovers the gold with surprise, and finally feels regret.
Tagore uses this small encounter to ask a large question: when we have a chance to give, how willing is our heart?
Think of one kind thing you could do today without expecting a reward.
That is a useful way to carry the poem's message into your own life.
